title: Count Distinct Substrings
directAnswer: Count how many distinct (unique) non-empty substrings a string has. There are n(n+1)/2 substrings counting duplicates; the answer subtracts the repeats. The clean optimal: build the suffix array, then the LCP array (Kasai), and compute n(n+1)/2 − Σ LCP[i]. Each suffix contributes (its length) new substrings minus the prefix it shares with the previous suffix in sorted order. That's O(n log n) for the suffix array plus O(n) for LCP.

remember.pattern: Suffix array + LCP: total substrings minus shared prefixes
remember.formula:
distinct = n*(n+1)/2 - sum(LCP[i] for i in 1..n-1)
  where SA = sorted suffixes, LCP[i] = longest common prefix of SA[i] and SA[i-1]
rules: Every substring is a **prefix of some suffix** — that reframing is the whole reason suffixes show up.
Sort the suffixes; adjacent sorted suffixes share the most prefix, so `LCP[i]` counts exactly the duplicate substrings to subtract.
Total substrings with duplicates is `n(n+1)/2`; distinct = that minus `Σ LCP`.
The O(n²) hashing baseline stores every substring's hash in a set — correct, but O(n²) time **and** space, and risks collisions without verification.
Use a separator-free input here; suffix arrays don't need one, unlike the Z/KMP concatenation trick.
whenToUse: Counting unique substrings, or unique substrings of a given length
Any problem reducible to 'distinct prefixes of suffixes'
Longest repeated substring, longest common substring of two strings
When you already need a suffix array/automaton for other queries
antiSignals: n is tiny (≤ a few thousand) and you just need a quick answer → the hashing set is simpler to write
You need online/streaming updates → suffix automaton incremental construction
Only counting occurrences of one fixed pattern → KMP/Z, not a full suffix structure
Memory is extremely tight → suffix array uses O(n) ints; a hash set of substrings is far worse
remember.takeaway: Two reframings carry the whole problem: substrings are prefixes of suffixes, and sorting suffixes makes duplicate prefixes adjacent. The LCP array then turns 'count distinct' into one subtraction.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can move past the brute-force hash set to the suffix-array + LCP formula, and whether you can explain why adjacent sorted suffixes capture all duplicate substrings.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Stopping at O(n²) hashing (and forgetting it's also O(n²) memory / collision-prone), or miscounting by forgetting that LCP is taken between adjacent suffixes in sorted order only.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive distinct = n(n+1)/2 − ΣLCP from first principles, mention the suffix automaton as the O(n) alternative, and note the same machinery solves longest-repeated-substring.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s` of length `n`, return the number of **distinct non-empty substrings** of `s`.

A substring is a contiguous slice `s[i..j]`. Two substrings are the same if they are equal as strings, regardless of where they occur. Count each distinct value once.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ (the optimal); the hashing baseline only survives n ≤ ~3000
Answer can be up to n(n+1)/2 ≈ 5×10⁹ for n = 10⁵ — use 64-bit
Substrings are contiguous; subsequences are a different problem
understanding: You're counting the size of the set of all contiguous slices. The duplicates are the difficulty: the naive count n(n+1)/2 over-counts repeated slices. The optimal solution recognizes that every substring is the prefix of exactly one suffix, sorts the suffixes so equal prefixes cluster, and subtracts the shared-prefix lengths (the LCP array) from the gross count.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Substrings or subsequences?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Substrings — contiguous. Subsequences are a separate, harder counting problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Empty substring counted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, count non-empty substrings only; that's why the gross total is n(n+1)/2.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Decides the approach. Up to a few thousand, hashing every substring is fine. For 10⁵, you need suffix array + LCP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the answer overflow 32-bit?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — for n = 10⁵ it reaches ~5×10⁹. Use a 64-bit accumulator.

examples.explanation: Substrings: "a", "aa", "aaa" — only 3 distinct even though there are 6 total slices.
All 6 slices are distinct: a, b, c, ab, bc, abc. No duplicates to subtract.
Distinct: a, b, ab, ba, aba, bab, abab. Gross 4·5/2 = 10; ΣLCP = 3, so 10 − 3 = 7.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Hash Every Substring
approaches.whenToMention: State it first; it defines correctness and motivates why we need a structure that avoids enumerating all n² substrings.

complexity.time: O(n²) average (hashing), O(n³) if comparing strings

hints: Enumerate every substring s[i..j] and insert it into a hash set; the set's size is the answer.
There are about n²/2 substrings. Inserting each O(1)-ish with a precomputed rolling hash gives O(n²); inserting raw strings costs an extra O(n) each.
Both the time and the memory grow as n² — that's the ceiling that suffix structures break.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n(n+1)/2 substrings. With a rolling/prefix hash, each substring's hash is O(1) to derive and O(1) to insert → O(n²) time. Storing them is O(n²) space. Comparing actual strings instead of hashes would add an O(n) factor (O(n³)).
approaches.explanation:
The definition-driven solution: produce every substring and let a set deduplicate.

**The literal method.** Loop `i` over start indices and `j` over end indices, and add `s[i..j]` to a set. After the loops, the set's cardinality is the count of distinct substrings.

**Making it O(n²) instead of O(n³).** Inserting the substring *string* costs O(length) for hashing and comparison, so the literal version is O(n³). Precompute prefix hashes so any substring's polynomial hash is O(1); store hashes in the set. That removes the per-substring length factor and gives O(n²) time — but introduces collision risk, so a fully correct version would verify or use double hashing.

**Why it doesn't scale.** Both time and memory are Θ(n²). At n = 10⁵ that's 10¹⁰ entries — neither the clock nor the heap survives. The approach is correct and is a fine sanity check for small n, but it enumerates exactly the thing we want to avoid enumerating.
approaches.insight: Hashing every substring treats each substring as independent, ignoring that substrings overlap massively. The suffix-array view exploits that overlap: equal substrings become equal prefixes of suffixes, which cluster when sorted.

approaches.name: Suffix Array + LCP (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Build to the formula distinct = n(n+1)/2 − ΣLCP and explain each piece.
hints: Reframe: every substring is a prefix of some suffix of s. So counting distinct substrings = counting distinct prefixes across all suffixes.
If you sort the suffixes, two suffixes that share a long prefix sit next to each other. The shared prefix is exactly the duplicated substrings between them.
Suffix i alone contributes (n − SA[i]) prefixes; subtract LCP[i], the prefix it shares with the previous sorted suffix, to avoid double counting. Summing gives n(n+1)/2 − ΣLCP.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Suffix array by prefix-doubling is O(n log n) (O(n log² n) with comparison sort, O(n log n) with radix). Kasai's LCP is O(n) amortized — the helper length h drops by at most 1 between steps. The final sum is O(n). Overall O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The optimal solution rests on two reframings and one formula.

**Reframing 1 — substrings are prefixes of suffixes.** Any substring `s[i..j]` is the prefix of length `j−i+1` of the suffix that starts at `i`. So the set of all substrings equals the set of all prefixes of all suffixes. Counting distinct substrings becomes counting distinct prefixes over every suffix.

**Reframing 2 — sort the suffixes.** Build the suffix array `SA`: the indices of all `n` suffixes sorted lexicographically. Why sort? Because two suffixes that begin with the same characters end up adjacent, so any prefix shared by two different suffixes is shared by *adjacent* sorted suffixes. That localizes all duplication to neighboring pairs.

**The LCP array does the counting.** `LCP[i]` is the length of the longest common prefix of `SA[i]` and `SA[i−1]` (consecutive sorted suffixes). Consider the suffixes in sorted order. The suffix at `SA[i]` has length `n − SA[i]`, contributing that many prefixes. But the first `LCP[i]` of those prefixes already appeared as prefixes of the previous suffix `SA[i−1]` — they're duplicates. So this suffix contributes `(n − SA[i]) − LCP[i]` *new* distinct substrings.

**The formula.** Summing the new contributions over all suffixes, the lengths sum to `n(n+1)/2` (each suffix's full length, which is just the gross count of all substrings) and the LCPs sum to the total duplication: `distinct = n(n+1)/2 − Σ LCP[i]`. The first suffix has no predecessor, so its LCP is 0 and it contributes its full length.

**Building the pieces efficiently.** The suffix array uses prefix doubling: rank suffixes by their first character, then repeatedly double the compared length using previous ranks, re-sorting by `(rank[i], rank[i+k])` pairs. That's `O(n log n)` ranks with `O(log n)` rounds. Kasai's algorithm computes LCP in `O(n)` by processing suffixes in original-string order and reusing the fact that the LCP can shrink by at most one when you move from suffix `i` to suffix `i+1`.

**An aside on the O(n) variant.** A suffix automaton counts distinct substrings in true `O(n)` by summing `len(state) − len(link(state))` over states. Mention it as the asymptotically tighter option; the suffix-array route is the more commonly expected derivation in interviews.
approaches.insight: The leap is seeing that 'distinct substrings' equals 'distinct prefixes of suffixes', because then sorting makes all duplicate prefixes adjacent and the LCP array measures exactly the over-count. The whole problem collapses to one subtraction: gross count minus shared prefixes.

pitfalls: Taking LCP between non-adjacent suffixes — only adjacent sorted pairs are correct.
Using a 32-bit accumulator for n(n+1)/2 — overflows for large n.
Computing rank from SA incorrectly in Kasai — rank[sa[i]] = i, not the reverse.
Forgetting that the first sorted suffix contributes its full length (LCP[0] = 0).

commonMistakes: Settling for the O(n²) hash set and ignoring that it's also O(n²) memory and collision-prone.
Computing LCP between suffixes that are not adjacent in sorted order.
Overflowing 32-bit on n(n+1)/2 for large inputs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Stopping at the hash-set baseline
commonMistakesDetailed.why: It enumerates all n²/2 substrings in both time and memory. For n = 10⁵ that is 10¹⁰ entries — it will not finish or fit. The interviewer expects the suffix-array reduction.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
seen = {s[i:j] for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n + 1)}
return len(seen)   # O(n^2) time AND memory

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong rank inversion in Kasai
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Kasai needs rank[i] = position of suffix i in SA. Writing sa[rank[i]] or inverting the assignment gives garbage LCPs.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) rank[i] = sa[i]; // WRONG direction
commonMistakesDetailed.good: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) rank[sa[i]] = i; // rank is the inverse of SA

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on the gross count
commonMistakesDetailed.why: n(n+1)/2 reaches ~5×10⁹ at n = 10⁵, past the 32-bit limit, so the subtraction underflows into a wrong (often negative) answer.

followupVariations.title: Longest Repeated Substring
followupVariations.hint: The maximum value in the LCP array is the length of the longest substring that appears at least twice.

followupVariations.title: Longest Common Substring of Two Strings
followupVariations.hint: Concatenate with a separator, build SA+LCP, take the max LCP between suffixes originating from different strings.

followupVariations.title: Count Distinct Substrings of Each Length
followupVariations.hint: Use the LCP array bucketed by length, or a suffix automaton's per-state contributions.

followupVariations.title: Distinct Substrings via Suffix Automaton (O(n))
followupVariations.hint: Sum len(state) − len(link(state)) over all states for a true linear-time count.

patternNote: Suffix Array + LCP. Recognise it for any 'distinct / repeated / common substring' question: the SA clusters equal prefixes and the LCP array measures their overlap, turning enumeration into arithmetic.
